I thought it would be a beautiful idea to take a small dose of LSD and visit an art museum. I'd read about people doing it. The first rooms were wonderful, the colours in the paintings glowed and moved. Then I came into a room with old religious paintings: martyrs, saints being tortured, the Last Judgement. The figures started to move. The saints turned their heads and looked at me. The demons in the Last Judgement crawled out of the frame. I could hear the screams of the damned.

I sat down on a bench in the middle of the room and couldn't get up. I felt that I was in the painting, being judged, and that I'd be sent down with the damned. A security guard came over and asked if I was okay, and his uniform and stern face made him look like one of the angels with swords. I said I was fine, but I was shaking. He asked if I needed a doctor, and I panicked and ran out of the museum. Outside, the statues on the façade were watching me. I sat in a park for hours under a tree, curled up, waiting for the judgement to end.

Ich bin auf Pilzen joggen gegangen, weil ich dachte, das wäre ein tolles Naturerlebnis. Nach ein paar Kilometern hatte ich das Gefühl, dass mein Herz aussetzt. Ich habe gespürt, wie es stolpert, dann ganz schnell schlägt, dann wieder stolpert. Ich bin stehen geblieben und habe mich an einen Baum gelehnt. Der Wald hat sich um mich gedreht. Ich war allein, weit weg von der Straße, und hatte panische Angst, dass ich hier an einem Herzstillstand sterbe und niemand mich findet. Ich habe mich hingesetzt und eine Ewigkeit lang meinen Puls gezählt, bis ich mich getraut habe, langsam zurückzugehen.

I'd been taking psychedelics for about ten years and considered myself experienced. I'd read all the books, done many trips, some difficult, and always come through. In hindsight, that confidence was dangerous.

I wanted to do what some people call a 'heroic' LSD trip: a very high dose, alone, in nature, with no music and no distractions. I rented a remote cabin in the mountains for a week in January. It had a woodstove and no phone signal. I told a friend where I was and that I'd call him when I got back to the village on the fifth day. I took about 1000ug on the second morning.

For the first hours it was overwhelming but also magnificent. The snow was glowing, the mountains were breathing, I felt that I was seeing the structure of the universe. I stood outside in the snow for a long time, barefoot I think, though I didn't notice the cold. I felt that I was the mountain, the snow, the sky, all at once.

At some point I lost the thread completely. There was no more 'I' who was seeing the mountain. There were no more mountains. There was a vast, white, silent field, and nothing in it. I don't know how long I was there. Hours, maybe. When something like a self came back, it didn't know what it was. I didn't know I was a human being. I had a body, but I didn't know what it was for. I didn't know what the cabin was, or what cold was, or what I was supposed to do.

The next thing I remember with any clarity is being inside the cabin, lying on the floor, and it was dark. The fire in the woodstove had gone out. I was shaking violently. My feet hurt in a strange, burning way and I couldn't feel my toes. I still didn't really know who I was, but my body knew that it was in danger. I crawled to the stove and tried to light it, but my hands didn't work properly. I couldn't figure out the matches. They kept turning into insects in my hand. It took me what felt like an hour to get a fire going.

Then the second wave hit, or maybe it was the cold and exhaustion. I spent the night in a kind of delirium, half on LSD, half in hypothermia. I saw figures in the corners of the cabin, tall and thin, standing silently. I talked to them. I asked them if I was dead. They didn't answer. At times I was sure that I had died out in the snow and that this cabin was some kind of waiting room. At other times I was sure I'd been in the cabin for years and would never leave.

When daylight came, I was still disoriented, but I knew my name again. My feet were swollen and blistered and some of my toes were white. I understood that I had frostbite. I couldn't walk to the village on those feet, it was eight kilometres. I spent two more days in the cabin, keeping the fire going, eating crackers, and trying to stay sane. I had no idea if my toes would have to be amputated. The LSD had worn off, but I was in a strange state, very fragile, with flashes of the white field whenever I closed my eyes.

On the fifth day, when I didn't call, my friend called the mountain rescue. They came on a snowmobile and found me. I spent a week in hospital. I lost the tips of two toes.

Ich habe LSD genommen und hatte plötzlich das Gefühl, dass meine verstorbenen Großeltern im Raum sind. Am Anfang war das schön, ich habe mich gefreut, sie zu sehen. Dann haben sie angefangen, mich anzuklagen. Sie haben mir vorgeworfen, dass ich sie im Altenheim kaum besucht habe, dass ich bei ihrer Beerdigung nicht geweint habe, dass ich ein schlechter Enkel bin. Ihre Stimmen wurden immer lauter, und ihre Gesichter wurden grau und eingefallen, so wie bei der Aufbahrung. Ich habe mich entschuldigt, immer wieder, aber sie haben nicht aufgehört. Ich hatte das Gefühl, vor einem Gericht zu stehen. Irgendwann bin ich aus der Wohnung gerannt und habe mich in den Hausflur gesetzt, weil ich dachte, dass sie mir dort nicht folgen können. Ich saß dort stundenlang im Dunkeln und habe geweint, bis ein Nachbar mich gefunden und gefragt hat, ob er jemanden anrufen soll.
Mushrooms. I saw myself as a baby being left alone in a cot for hours, crying, nobody coming. It felt very real and very lonely.

I was at a party in a squat with ketamine and LSD going around. I'd taken both. Around 3am the police raided the building. There were maybe 20 officers in riot gear, with dogs. They came in shouting, with torches, and everyone panicked. I was in a k-hole on a mattress in a back room, barely able to move. Through the LSD, the officers looked like giant black insects with glowing eyes. One of them grabbed me by the arm and pulled me up, and I couldn't stand, so he dragged me. I was sure I was being taken to be executed. They made us all sit on the floor of the main hall with our hands on our heads. The dogs were barking right next to my face. Someone next to me was crying. I kept slipping in and out of the room in my head, sometimes I was there, sometimes I was floating in a dark void, and every time I came back, the dogs and the torches were still there. They searched us and took our names. I was released at dawn without charges. I walked home barefoot because someone had taken my shoes.

Ich war mit meiner Freundin auf Pilzen im Park, als mich eine Wespe in den Hals gestochen hat. Ich habe eine Wespenallergie, wusste aber nicht, wie schlimm sie ist. Innerhalb von Minuten ist mein Hals zugeschwollen, ich bekam kaum noch Luft, und mein ganzer Körper hat gejuckt. Ich hatte meinen Notfallpen nicht dabei. Durch die Pilze hatte ich das Gefühl, dass sich mein Hals in eine Schlange verwandelt, die mich erwürgt. Meine Freundin hat den Notruf gewählt, und ich lag auf dem Rasen, rang nach Luft und war mir sicher, dass ich sterbe. Die Sanitäter haben mir eine Spritze gegeben und mich ins Krankenhaus gebracht. Ich war noch Stunden unter Wirkung und habe die ganze Zeit gedacht, dass mein Hals wieder zugeht.

This is about the night my son was born. I'm still not sure how to talk about it.

My wife was 36 weeks pregnant. Her due date was a month away, and we'd agreed that I would have one last 'free' weekend with my best friends before the baby. We went to a cabin about three hours away, and on the Saturday evening we took LSD. My wife knew I was going and what I was planning. She was fine with it; I'd done it a few times before and it had always been okay.

Around 10pm, at the peak, my phone rang. It was my wife. Her waters had broken. She was having contractions and was on her way to the hospital in a taxi. She was scared and asked me to come right away.

I will never forget the feeling of that moment. Everything in the room seemed to fall apart. I couldn't understand what she was saying at first. Her voice was coming through in waves of colour. When I finally understood, I felt like I'd been struck by lightning. None of us could drive. We were three hours away, in the middle of nowhere. I was tripping harder than I ever had.

One of my friends called a taxi from the nearest town. It took an hour to arrive. During that hour I was walking in circles around the cabin, crying, calling my wife over and over. She stopped answering. I was sure something had gone terribly wrong. I saw images of her bleeding, of a tiny blue baby. I saw myself at a double funeral. I felt that the universe was punishing me for choosing to get high instead of being with my family.

The taxi ride was two and a half hours. My friend came with me. I sat in the back seat with my eyes closed because the headlights of oncoming cars were unbearable, like being stabbed. The driver had the radio on and every song seemed to be about death or loss. I was praying, which I never do. My friend kept saying 'she's going to be okay', and his voice sounded hollow and fake to me.

We arrived at the hospital around 2am. I was still clearly under the influence. I knew it and I was terrified that the staff would notice. I went to the maternity ward and a midwife told me my wife was in the delivery room, that the labour was progressing fast and that I could go in. I washed my face with cold water and went in.

My wife was in the middle of it, in pain, exhausted. She looked at me and I think she knew immediately. I held her hand. The room was too bright, the machines were beeping, the midwife's face kept shifting. I was trying with every part of me to be present and useful, but I was also seeing things: the walls breathing, colours flowing from my wife's body. At one point the baby's heart rate dropped and the midwife called a doctor, and there were suddenly four people in the room and a lot of urgent talking. I was completely sure our son was dying. I felt like I was going to faint. I sat down on the floor in the corner.

He was born about twenty minutes later, healthy, after a vacuum delivery. They put him on my wife's chest and he cried, and I cried, and it should have been the most beautiful moment of my life. In a way it was. But it was also mixed with the remnants of the LSD, the shame, and the terror of the previous hours. When they gave him to me, I was afraid to hold him, afraid I'd drop him, afraid that my hands weren't real. His face kept changing in my arms.
LSD. Ich hatte plötzlich das Gefühl, dass alle Menschen auf der Welt tot sind und nur ich übrig bin, und dass die Leute um mich herum nur Erinnerungen sind.

I booked a float tank session and decided, stupidly, to take a moderate dose of mushrooms beforehand. In the tank, in total darkness and silence, floating in body-temperature water, I lost all sense of where my body was. Very quickly I didn't know if I had a body at all. I felt that I'd dissolved into the water and that the water was infinite. I couldn't find the walls of the tank. I panicked and splashed and got salt water in my eyes, which burned terribly. I couldn't find the door or the light switch. I was sure I was drowning in an endless black sea. I started screaming. The staff came after a few minutes and opened the tank. The light was blinding. I was shaking and crying and couldn't explain what was wrong. They sat with me in the lobby until I could leave.

Took acid before an eight-hour coach trip, thinking I'd sleep. Couldn't sleep, felt trapped in the coach with strangers, the motion made me sick and the toilet was disgusting. Hours of claustrophobia and nausea.

Ich war bei einer Freundin zu Besuch, und wir haben zusammen Pilze genommen, während ihr Partner unterwegs war. Er kam früher als erwartet nach Hause, betrunken, und als er merkte, dass wir Pilze genommen hatten, ist er völlig ausgerastet. Er hat herumgebrüllt, gegen die Wand geschlagen und meine Freundin am Arm gepackt und geschüttelt. Ich saß auf dem Sofa und konnte mich nicht bewegen. Sein Gesicht hat sich in eine Fratze verwandelt, und seine Stimme war so laut, dass ich dachte, mein Kopf platzt. Ich hatte das Gefühl, dass er uns beide umbringen wird. Meine Freundin hat geweint und versucht, ihn zu beruhigen. Irgendwann hat er mich angeschrien, ich solle verschwinden. Ich bin barfuß aus der Wohnung gelaufen und stand auf der Straße, unter voller Wirkung, und wusste nicht, was ich tun soll. Ich habe dann die Polizei gerufen. Als sie kamen, war er schon ruhiger, und meine Freundin hat gesagt, es sei alles in Ordnung. Ich habe mich die ganze Nacht schuldig gefühlt, weil ich sie dort zurückgelassen habe, und gleichzeitig war ich wütend, dass sie ihn verteidigt hat.
